reasoning_traces.think:
Nearest neighbor classification operates on the principle of assigning a query point to the class most prevalent among its k nearest neighbors in feature space. This method relies on local similarity measures such as Euclidean distance. Its failure mode arises from the curse of dimensionality where distances become less meaningful. Linear Discriminant Analysis (LDA) seeks optimal projections that maximize inter-class separation while minimizing intra-class variance. It assumes normally distributed classes with equal covariance matrices. When these assumptions fail, LDA may misclassify due to biased projections. Principal Component Analysis (PCA) reduces dimensionality by identifying principal components capturing maximum variance. While PCA is effective for noise reduction and visualization, it lacks class discrimination. These primitives form a hierarchy: nearest neighbor provides non-parametric local inference, LDA enables parametric discriminative projection, and PCA offers foundational low-rank representation. Each builds upon statistical independence and metric structure, yet diverges in handling complexity and generalization.
